newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - France banks on growth to turn jobless tide.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France banks on growth to turn jobless tide.

text.p: The French government, confronted with a further rise in unemployment in the first month of 1997, said on Friday the economy was looking up and this would produce jobs, but shied from predicting when jobless queues would fall.

Despite several positive indicators for stronger growth in the economy at the outset of 1997, the centre-right government is still plagued by the politically sensitive issue of record unemployment as it gives priority to belt-tightening in a key year of preparation for European economic and monetary union.

The labour ministry said unemployment had risen by 18,100 in January to just short of 3.1 million and that the unemployment rate based on International Labour Organisation (ILO) criteria was stuck at the record 12.7 percent hit in November.

The rise follows a drop of 29,000 in December but economists have dismissed that decrease, and another drop last October, as "statistical blips" and say unemployment is still on the rise. Some say it could reach 13 percent later this year.
The government is hoping for economic growth of at least 2.3 percent in 1997, after a relatively poor 1.3 percent increase in 1996, and banking on the increased growth to create jobs.

So far this year, its predictions of an economic upturn have been bolstered by news of rising consumer spending and surveys showing that French industrialists are more optimistic about the prospects for an increase in production in the coming months, and news that France had another record trade surplus in 1996.

Labour minister Jaques Barrot told state radio on Friday it was still hard to decipher the pattern but that the economy was looking healthier, with rising household spending and exports, and signs companies were starting to reinvest and recruit.
"Jobs come from growth. Growth is coming back, consumption and exports are picking up. Company bosses are starting to invest again and then recruiting," he told France Inter radio.

"It's a bit like the tide. In terms of jobs we don't quite know where we stand at the moment, whether the tide is rising or falling. It's tricky because the direction of the waves is not clear," he said. "But in the opening months of 1997 we will probably be stuck with upward and downward spikes," he added.

Comforting Barrot's thesis amid the prevailing gloom, the UNEDIC agency which distributes unemployment benefit said economic growth could limit the jobless rise to 15,000 for 1997 as a whole and lead to a fall for 30,000 next year.
The January unemployment data showed a drop for the second month in a row in the number of jobless men and women aged 25 or less, with a 1.5 percent drop for men and 0.7 percent for women.
